commentary.bottom_line: No study has tested whether defining explainability needs with end users or tailoring transparency information by role improves use, trust calibration, or patient outcomes. Three small simulated studies of clinicians suggest that explanation preferences and their effect on trust vary by person, specialty, and expertise, which supports the hazard but not the remedy.

perspectives.view: Nine sources endorse the practice, and most are commentaries or consensus guidance. No study tests it. Three hazard studies in offline settings, with 54, 27, and 10 clinicians, report poor agreement on preferred explanation methods (Fleiss' kappa 0.049) and differences by expertise and specialty. Small samples and indirect outcomes would limit certainty even for the hazard.

In one study, 72% of infectious disease clinicians preferred SHAP explanations, compared with 44% of emergency medicine clinicians, and 36% of emergency clinicians favored AraucanaXAI. A second study found that the effect of explanations on trust depended on the scenario and on staff expertise. This suggests tailoring may need to go below broad role categories, but no study measured workflow burden or fidelity.

The hazard studies measured stated preferences, agreement, and trust. None measured decision errors, overreliance, or harm reaching patients. The record therefore does not show whether mismatched explanations cause unsafe decisions or whether tailored explanations prevent them.

Several endorsing sources name patients as a group with distinct information needs. All three studies enrolled only clinicians, so no evidence describes what patients want to know about an AI tool or whether tailored information helps them understand its role in their care.

commentary.research_gap: Controlled studies should compare role-tailored transparency materials with a single standard version in live clinical use. They should measure decision accuracy, appropriate reliance, time burden, and patient comprehension, and they should include patients and nonphysician staff as participants.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice. The three hazard studies enrolled clinicians in the United Kingdom, Italy, and eight unnamed countries and did not include Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The information needs of these patients and the staff who serve them remain unstudied, so tailoring guidance for them would rest on assumption rather than data.
